meta: Li Song's album leaf The Knickknack Peddler, in which children attack a snake while the peddler rushes over.
about: Children attack a snake with a stick and a stone while the peddler rushes toward them, leaving his goods unwatched. Li Song, a court artist from Hangzhou, was known for fine paintings of children, peddlers and their wares. The Cleveland Museum of Art notes that it was painted under the emperor Ningzong, and that the danger to the children may allude to his nine sons, who died young and left him without a male heir. Look near the top of the left basket for an upside down skull.
credit_line: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund

meta: Sahib Ram's painting of a Shvetambara Jain teacher instructing laypeople, made in the mid-1700s.
about: A Jain teacher sits before a manuscript on a low table, one hand raised in the gesture of discourse and the other holding a cloth over his mouth to keep out insects. Men of the audience gather near the front and women sit in a group toward the back. The teacher and the white-clad men behind him are householder monks, who could grow hair and moustaches and wear a coloured shawl showing higher status. In Rajasthan such monks often worked as scribes and kept manuscript libraries.
credit_line: Purchase and partial gift from the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection; Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund

meta: Chen Juzhong's album leaf The Autumn Hunt, from a Chinese genre of paintings of foreign people hunting.
about: The rider at the left wears a typical Qidan hairstyle, with the head shaved on top and thin braids below. Chen Juzhong painted this album leaf on silk around 1200. Riding and hunting were especially popular among the Khitan and the Jurchen, peoples who lived along China's northeastern border. The Chinese court was intrigued by their nomadic way of life, and artists developed a genre of paintings of foreign people hunting. The Cleveland Museum of Art owns this one.

meta: Mushfiq's album leaf of Zulaykha and Joseph from a Persian poem by Jami, painted in the Deccan for a Mughal minister.
about: Two episodes from the story of Joseph and Zulaykha share this page. In the first, Zulaykha waits in a house she has built for Joseph, with romantic scenes painted on its walls. The virtuous Joseph, shown with a flaming halo and an ever youthful face, rejects her. In the second, many years later, she is an elderly widow, and his prayers will restore her beauty so that the two can finally be joined. The painter Mushfiq slipped his name and the date into a brick of the house at upper left.
credit_line: Gift in honor of Madeline Neves Clapp; Gift of Mrs. Henry White Cannon by exchange; Bequest of Louise T. Cooper; Leonard C. Hanna Jr. Fund; From the Catherine and Ralph Benkaim Collection

meta: Tao Hong's silk album leaf of farmers returning home on a spring evening, from the early 1600s.
about: Farmers walk home after a day in the fields, past a shallow stream and dormant rice fields. Returning birds and light sprinkles of green on the trees show that the farming season is beginning, and the Cleveland Museum of Art reads them as a sign of hope for a good harvest. Tao Hong, an artist the museum calls versatile but little known today, used light colours and fine brushwork to give the scene a feeling of natural light. A companion leaf shows a lone crane in a bamboo grove.
credit_line: Gift of Dr. and Mrs. Sherman E. Lee

meta: Victor Higgins's 1920 watercolor of a dry arroyo, painted with the landscape of Taos, New Mexico, in mind.
about: Dry stream bed and desert hills fill this watercolor of an arroyo. Victor Higgins lived in Taos, New Mexico, after 1914 and found inspiration in its dramatic landscape. The Smithsonian American Art Museum says he stressed the patterns and textures of the ground and gave the local plants an abstract treatment. He painted with a relatively dry brush and let the whiteness of the paper add to the feeling of sun-parched land. |||

meta: Yao Shou's magpie from the handscroll Pillars of the Country, painted in 1494 in ink with a poem in his own hand.
about: A magpie perches on a bare branch with its beak open as if singing, and bamboo leaves rise below it. It is one of six images Yao Shou painted along a handscroll, together with a riverscape and other natural subjects. The Art Institute of Chicago places it in the bird-and-flower genre, which prized realism, but calls Yao's vision more personal. He used varied tones of black ink, painted the bamboo in free strokes of pale blue, and added a poem in cursive script signed with his courtesy name, Gongshou.

meta: Yōgetsu's hanging scroll of Sugawara Michizane, the exiled Kyoto aristocrat honoured as the deity Tenjin.
about: Sugawara Michizane sits in a dark robe and tall black court cap, with three columns of poetry above him. He was a Kyoto aristocrat who died in exile in Dazaifu on Kyushu after being slandered at court. Shrines were later built to pacify his vengeful spirit. Zen painting took his image into its repertoire of enlightened figures. The monk Yōgetsu of Kyushu painted this scroll, and the monk Sakugen Shūryō inscribed it with a Chinese-style poem, an ode to Michizane as the deity Tenjin.
credit_line: Gift from the Collection of George Gund III

meta: Francesco Bonsignori's Saint Sebastian, a Florentine panel that passed through the Lanz collection and Hitler's planned Linz museum.
about: Saint Sebastian stands bound to a post, with arrows through his body and small streams of blood on his chest and legs. The Amsterdam professor Otto Lanz bought the panel from the dealer Luigi Grassi in Florence in 1909. In 1941 his widow sold it with other paintings to Hans Posse for Adolf Hitler's planned museum in Linz. It was recovered after the war, on 20 October 1945.

meta: Francesco Panini's watercolor of St. Peter's Basilica lit by a cross of oil lamps on Holy Thursday.
about: A great cross made of several hundred lit oil lamps hangs in front of Bernini's canopy in St. Peter's Basilica on Holy Thursday. Francesco Panini shows the view from a spot between the left aisle and the nave, which makes the composition asymmetrical. Small figures stand under the cross and are scattered around the nave. The drawing is in watercolor and ink. |||

meta: Frederic Edwin Church's Niagara, a view of the Horseshoe Falls now in the National Gallery of Art.
about: Rainbow spray rises from the broad curve of the Horseshoe Falls, with rough rapids in the foreground. Frederic Edwin Church sold the painting the year he made it to the New York firm of Williams, Stevens and Williams, and it was forfeited to the bankers Brown Brothers. At a charity sale in December 1861, John Taylor Johnston bought it. The Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington purchased it later, and the National Gallery of Art acquired it in 2014. Wikipedia calls it Church's most important work of its time.

meta: Whistler's full-length study of a young woman in a yellow-gray cloak, titled Effie Deans after a novel by Walter Scott.
about: A young woman in an olive-yellow hooded cloak and long gray skirt stands in profile, facing right, against a dark background. Maud Franklin, a painter herself and Whistler's partner, posed for it and for several other standing women he titled Arrangement in the mid 1870s. The extra title Effie Deans, after a character in Walter Scott's novel The Heart of Midlothian, was first used in 1886. The inscription and signature were probably added only in 1889.

meta: Honoré Daumier's Wandering Saltimbanques, an oil sketch on wood owned by the Rouart family and left to the National Gallery of Art.
about: Dark, loosely brushed figures crowd a shallow stage. A man in a white ruffled collar and tall cap stands before a bare-chested figure who carries a ladder on his shoulders. Honoré Daumier painted it on wood. Alexis Rouart of Paris owned it by 1901, when he lent it to a Daumier exhibition, and a red wax seal with his name is on the back. It probably went by inheritance to his father, Henri Rouart. Chester Dale bought it in 1933 and left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1963.

meta: Paul Cezanne's portrait of Antony Valabrègue, a bearded man in a dark suit, now in the National Gallery of Art.
about: A bearded man in a dark suit and waistcoat sits with his hands together against a loosely brushed dark ground. The dealer Ambroise Vollard had the portrait first and sold it in 1901 to a buyer named Breysse, who sold it back three years later. In 1911 it went through Bernheim-Jeune to Auguste Pellerin, and it then passed by inheritance to his son Jean-Victor. Paul Mellon bought it in 1966 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Vincent van Gogh's Roulin's Baby, a painting of an infant in a white bonnet, left to the National Gallery of Art by Chester Dale.
about: An infant in a white bonnet with blue trim sits against a pale green background, painted with thick brushwork. The first owner on record is Mme Jules Armand, born Joséphine Ronin, of Arles. A story said that van Gogh gave it to the hospital in Arles where he stayed, which later sold it, but a letter of 1966 from the hospital director says the hospital never owned it. Dealers in Amsterdam, Paris and New York handled it. Chester Dale bought it on 9 March 1927 and left it to the National Gallery of Art in 1963.

meta: Winslow Homer's The Dinner Horn, an 1870 painting of a young woman blowing a horn on a lawn, given to the National Gallery of Art.
about: A young woman in a white dress stands with her back to us on a lawn beside a weathered wooden house, blowing a long dinner horn. Fallen leaves lie on the ground, and a cow grazes in the field beyond. A 1981 sale catalogue says Winslow Homer gave the picture to Charles Collins and that it descended in the Collins family. It was bought in at that sale, then passed through dealers to the collector Richard Manoogian. Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon bought it in 1985 and gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1994.
credit_line: Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Paul Mellon

meta: Robert Jones's design for the west-wall chimney-piece of the music room in the Royal Pavilion, Brighton.
about: Two tall pagoda-style towers flank a fluted column on this watercolor and pencil design for a chimney-piece in the music room of the Royal Pavilion in Brighton. Robert Jones drew the joints as short circular columns with bases and capitals of conjoined lotus leaves. The cornice rests in the centre on the spread wings of a dragon. A pair of porcelain pagodas and a clock decorate the mantel. The colonnettes at right are slightly different in design. |||

meta: Antonie Sminck Pitloo's 1820 view through the Janus arch to San Giorgio in Velabro in Rome.
about: Through the arch of the Janus Quadrifrons in Rome, the view reaches the church of San Giorgio in Velabro. Two figures kneel in the passage before a priest who leads a procession toward the church. Antonie Sminck Pitloo signed and dated the picture at lower left in 1820. Small figures rest in the foreground beside a shallow puddle, and a brick bell tower rises beyond.

meta: Jean-Louis Forain's pastel sketch of a woman and child, found in 1979 as the backing of another Forain.
about: A woman in a dark hat looks toward the viewer, and a child's head rests against her shoulder below her. Jean-Louis Forain made this pastel and chalk sketch on canvas. Lessing J. Rosenwald of Jenkintown, Pennsylvania, gave it to the National Gallery of Art in 1943. In 1979 conservators found that the canvas had served as the backing for another Forain, a pastel on paper.

meta: Lluís Borrassà's panel of Saint Andrew refusing to worship the idol, in the Museo del Prado.
about: A gilded idol stands at the centre of the panel on a tall structure under a Gothic canopy. Lluís Borrassà used it to divide the scene into two groups, which the Prado says avoids a cramped feeling. On the left the proconsul Agen sits on a high throne with two men at his feet. On the right Saint Andrew is led in as a prisoner by soldiers and executioners. |||
